segments: A gaming compatibility layer extensively customized by Valve on top of Wine. This article distinguishes official Proton, GE extensions, and gaming-platform runtimes. Wayland, HDR, DLL upgrades, and frame generation all require compatible versions, drivers, and games.
Proton's technology stack: the graphics translation quartet
Proton deeply integrates the following core components on top of Wine:

DXVK is an important component through which Proton handles several types of Direct3D graphics calls. Compared with WineD3D's different implementation approach, it can improve the following in some games:
Lower CPU overhead for draw calls
More precise GPU memory management
Asynchronous compute capabilities on modern GPUs

Jointly maintained by Valve and CodeWeavers. D3D12 games running through this Proton path, such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake 2, depend on this component. DXR support also depends on VKD3D-Proton, the driver, GPU extensions, and the game.
DXVK-NVAPI — NVIDIA-specific translation

Translates NVIDIA NVAPI calls into corresponding Linux interfaces, enabling DLSS, RTX ray tracing, and Reflex low latency under Proton. NVAPI, DLSS, ray tracing, and Reflex each have different requirements; DXVK-NVAPI is not a universal switch that gives any GPU NVIDIA-exclusive features. Check the driver requirements for the component version and the game's support, rather than reducing all capabilities to a single minimum driver version.
FAudio — XAudio2 audio
Windows games use XAudio2 for audio processing; FAudio is an open-source reimplementation.

Using Proton independently of Steam
Complete workflow: setting up non-Steam games through umu

GE explicitly states that running non-Steam games outside Steam is supported only through umu, which provides the complete Proton runtime/container environment. Calling proton run directly from an extracted directory may omit required runtime libraries and the container environment, and is not a generally supported approach. For managers with umu integration, verify the backend actually in use; the application name alone is not enough.

The following assumes that umu-run has been installed using your distribution's method and that a fixed GE-Proton version has been extracted into a user-owned directory. <version> is a version placeholder to replace. On NixOS, install tools through the project configuration instead of copying package-manager commands from other distributions.

Choose GAMEID from the umu database for the target game to apply its corresponding protonfixes. umu-default is a teaching value that does not specify a particular game identity and does not guarantee any specific fixes. Set STORE according to the game's source as well. Automatic selection with PROTONPATH=GE-Proton can download a changing version, but this mode must not be described as pinned and reproducible.

Prefix management and custom configuration
Viewing and managing Steam game prefixes

Each Steam library has its own steamapps/compatdata/<APPID>/. The actual Wine prefix is usually in its pfx/ subdirectory. STEAM_COMPAT_DATA_PATH points to the parent compatibility-data directory managed by Proton, while WINEPREFIX points to the Wine prefix; the two are not interchangeable. Paths may also differ for Flatpak Steam, additional libraries, or non-Steam shortcuts.

If supported by a particular version, WINETRICKS_RUN_AS_ROOT bypasses the protection against running as Linux root; it does not enable Windows administrator mode. Do not enable it to solve application-permission problems, and do not start Wine/Proton with sudo. Use a regular user account and address the correct prefix, file permissions, and application requirements.

If you genuinely need to rebuild, first close Steam and game-related processes, verify backups of saves, cloud-sync data, and third-party licenses, then rename the entire compatibility-data directory to preserve it. Replace and verify <APPID> and the library path below first:
Launching again may recreate the compatibility data, but unsynced saves or application state will not reappear on their own. Verify the new directory before deciding how long to keep the old backup.
Customizing prefix configuration for non-Steam games

For games managed by umu, use the configuration tools from the same runner, for example by opening winecfg through its winetricks entry point. Avoid inadvertently letting a different host Wine version update the prefix.
Set the required reported Windows version under Applications. Changing only the registry's ProductName text does not change Wine's emulated version or API behavior.

If you need a configuration file, use keys supported by the actual DXVK version and point DXVK_CONFIG_FILE to a file the application can access. Seeing the HUD does not prove that every graphics feature or performance across an entire play session has been verified.

Installing Proton-GE

For Steam, choose a specific version and matching architecture asset from the official GE Releases. Verify its checksum/provenance, then extract it into compatibilitytools.d/ for the current Steam installation. The path differs between native packages, Flatpak Steam, and distribution layouts; do not blindly copy another system's directory.

After restarting Steam, verify the actual runner in the game's compatibility properties. If you use ProtonUp-Qt, also check the target Steam installation, downloaded version, and directory. It is a management tool, not a performance guarantee. On NixOS, the GE package can be managed through pinned nixpkgs and the Steam module, avoiding confusion with identically named versions in manually managed directories. For use outside Steam, follow the umu support scope described above.

Steam Deck verification

Valve's verification targets the Steam Deck's hardware, software, and interaction conditions. It is a useful reference, but it does not guarantee that a different desktop Linux system's GPU, drivers, input, display, and third-party launchers will all work. Also read the specific reasons for the rating and check the current game version.
System optimization suggestions

Kernel and synchronization: First establish which synchronization path the actual runner uses. Check NTSYNC device availability, permissions, and build support separately; do not choose based solely on the kernel major version.

Drivers: Check the requirements of the DXVK/VKD3D-Proton versions and the game you use. Verify the versions and bitness of NVIDIA proprietary drivers or AMD/Intel Mesa separately; no single set of minimum version numbers remains valid forever.
GameMode/MangoHud: Install through your distribution or Nix configuration, verify that the tools work, then use gamemoderun %command% or mangohud %command% in the game's launch options.

Memory mappings: Read vm.max_map_count and inspect failure logs to determine whether the limit is being exhausted; do not unconditionally set an enormous value. If a change is necessary, choose the value using current evidence for the distribution/game, and record the previous value and rollback method.
Shader pre-caching: Test cold-versus-warm startup behavior for your current Steam, driver, and game versions. Caching does not eliminate all shader compilation during gameplay.

%command% in launch options is a Steam placeholder, not a Bash program that can be pasted directly into a normal terminal. Change one condition at a time, recording the runner, driver, test scenario, frame times, and results after reverting.

Version boundaries: At the time of verification, the GE README marked PROTON_FSR4_RDNA3_UPGRADE as obsolete and ineffective; supported RDNA3 hardware also uses PROTON_FSR4_UPGRADE. Valve's current README marks PROTON_NO_ESYNC as obsolete in Proton 11.0. Variables in older tutorials can still help explain historical behavior, but the README for the selected release is authoritative. One variable alone does not establish that media, Wayland, HDR, XeSS, or other extensions are working.
